title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about finding and using sources at university: what searching really means, and how to do it well. By the end you will be able to explain what academic searching is and how it differs from everyday searching, describe what makes a search effective, and plan a simple search by choosing keywords for it.

This is not a skill you can skip. Almost every assignment asks you to find and use sources, and the quality of what you find shapes the quality of what you write. Searching well saves you time and leads you to better material than the first result you happen to land on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what academic searching is and how it differs from everyday searching
describe the principles of an effective, planned search
plan a simple search and identify keywords for it.

title: In real academic practice
body: Finding and using sources is the groundwork of academic study. Every essay built on reading, every literature review, every project that rests on evidence begins with a search. Build the habit now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the research and fact-finding that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what academic searching is: how it differs from the searching you already do every day. Second, the principles of effective searching: the stages a good search moves through. Third, planning and keywords: the first practical moves of a search you plan yourself. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

title: Orientation
body: You search for things every day. You type a question into Google, or ask a voice assistant, and you get an answer in seconds. Searching for your studies feels like it should be the same, but it is not. This lesson looks at what academic searching really is, so that finding sources for your work stops being hit and miss and starts being something you can do on purpose.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and searching for academic sources may be new. At this stage you are not expected to master library databases or advanced search tools. The aim is to understand what academic searching is, and how it differs from the everyday searching you already do, so you have firm ground to build on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what 'searching' means in an academic context
distinguish academic searching from everyday searching
recognise academic searching in {{context}} as exploratory, iterative and strategy-driven.

title: Concept: definition
body:
At a basic level, searching simply means looking for information. That covers checking a fact online as much as finding sources for an essay. What makes academic searching different is not the looking, but how you go about it.

Academic searching is exploratory: you are following a question whose answer you are still working out, not fetching a single fact. It is iterative: you try some words, see what comes back, and search again with better ones. And it is strategy-driven: you decide what you are looking for, and how, before you start. This lesson is about that difference; the lessons that follow are about how you do it.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that academic searching is planned and strategic, not a quick lookup. This lesson is about what a good search actually involves. An effective search is not luck or speed: it moves through a set of stages, and knowing them turns searching from guesswork into something you can get right on purpose.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to master each stage yet. Some, such as using a library discovery service, evaluating sources and extending a search, are skills that later courses build in full. The aim here is to recognise the whole shape of an effective search, so you know what good practice looks like.

title: Learning outcomes

_items.text: describe the stages of an effective search
recognise effective searching as a planned process rather than a one-off lookup
identify effective search practice in a worked example set in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Effective searching is a process, not a single action. A good search moves through recognisable stages: you plan what you are looking for, identify the keywords that capture it, use your library's search tool with care, weigh the sources you find, and extend the search to reach further material.

What matters most at this stage is the shape of the whole, not mastery of each part. A one-off lookup that stops at the first result skips almost all of this. A planned search works through the stages, which is why it reaches better material and wastes less of your time. The later stages are skills that other courses develop; here the point is to see how they fit together.

title: Orientation
body: You have seen that academic searching is planned, and that an effective search moves through stages. This lesson takes the first two stages and makes them practical. Before you search, you plan; and the heart of the plan is choosing your keywords. Get these right and the rest of the search has a real chance of working.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to build a complex search with advanced tools yet. The aim is to plan a simple search, set a clear objective, and pick sensible keywords, including a synonym or two. These are the first moves of every search, and they are enough to find useful material on most topics.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: plan a search by setting an objective and considering source type and date
identify keywords for a search topic
give a synonym for a keyword in {{context}} to broaden a search.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Planning a search starts with a simple question: what am I actually looking for? Reflecting on what you already know helps you set an objective and decide what sort of source would answer it, and how recent that source needs to be.

The plan then turns into keywords. Keywords are the words or short phrases you search with, and they drive the search: the tool looks for the words you give it, so the words you choose decide what you find. Because one idea can be named in more than one way, it helps to think of synonyms. A synonym is a word that means much the same as another, such as 'car' and 'automobile'. Adding synonyms broadens a search so you do not miss material that uses different words for the same idea.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Pick a topic from your own course. What is your search objective, and what three keywords would you start with? Can you think of a synonym for any of them?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A search begins with a plan: an objective, and a thought about what sort of source you need and how recent it should be. The plan becomes keywords, the words that drive the search, and synonyms broaden it so you catch the same idea under different words. You can now plan a simple search, identify keywords, and give a synonym to widen your results. With this, you are ready to search on purpose.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Everyday searching, academic searching
body: Four cards on what makes academic searching different from the searching you already do. Read each one.
instruction: Read through the cards below. Work through all four.
ariaRegion: Information cards comparing everyday and academic searching.

_items.title: More than a lookup
_items.subtitle: What searching is
_items.text: At heart, searching just means looking for information. Academic searching is still that, but it looks for material you can trust and build an argument on, not a single quick fact.

_items.title: Exploratory
_items.subtitle: The answer is not known yet
_items.text: Everyday searching often fetches one fact. Academic searching follows a question whose answer you are still working out, so you expect to read around a topic rather than land on one result.

_items.title: Iterative
_items.subtitle: You search again
_items.text: A first search rarely gives you what you need. Academic searching is iterative: you try words, see what returns, and adjust and search again, rather than giving up when the first attempt disappoints.

_items.title: Strategy-driven
_items.subtitle: You plan it
_items.text: Everyday searching is quick and unplanned. Academic searching is driven by a strategy: you decide what you are looking for, and how to look, before you start typing.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two students given the same essay question and told to find sources for it.

{{learner-a}} types the whole essay question into a search box, glances at the first few results, and picks the one at the top. The search is over in a minute. But {{learner-a}} has treated this like looking up a fact: one attempt, no plan, and whatever came first. There was no sense of what a good source would look like or how to look again. This is everyday searching.

{{learner-b}} starts by asking what the question is really about and what sort of source would answer it. {{learner-b}} tries a few keywords, sees what comes back, and searches again with better words when the first set is too broad. The search takes longer, but it is exploratory, iterative and planned. This is academic searching.

Both students searched. Only {{learner-b}} treated searching as a discipline rather than a quick lookup.

title: Search like an academic
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These habits turn everyday searching into academic searching. Try them on your next search.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I worked out what my search is actually for, before typing anything?
Have I thought about what sort of source would answer it?
Have I searched with a few chosen words, rather than the whole question?
When the results were poor, did I try again with different words?
Have I read around the topic rather than stopping at the first result?
Have I noticed when I am treating an academic search like a quick lookup?

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The stages of an effective search
body: An effective search moves through five stages. Step through them to see how a good search is built.
instruction: Step through each stage to see what it involves.

_items.title: Plan your search
_items.body: Reflect on what you already know and set a clear objective. What are you actually looking for, and what sort of source would answer it? This is where an effective search begins.

_items.title: Identify keywords
_items.body: Pick the words and short phrases that capture your topic. Keywords drive the search, so changing them changes what you find. Thinking of synonyms widens what you can reach.

_items.title: Use your discovery service
_items.body: Search your library's discovery tool with care, so you look deliberately rather than hoping for the best. A later course develops this skill in full.

_items.title: Evaluate your sources
_items.body: Weigh what you find rather than taking the first results. Is the source suitable, current and trustworthy for your purpose? A later course develops this in full.

_items.title: Extend your search
_items.body: Follow leads from what you find to reach further material, so your search grows rather than stopping at the first page. A later course develops this in full.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are asked to find sources on the same topic for a seminar.

{{learner-a}} opens the library search tool, types the topic in, and uses the first article on the list. The job feels done. But {{learner-a}} skipped almost every stage: no plan, no thought about keywords, no weighing of the source, and no second look. It was one lookup, and whatever came first. This is a one-off lookup, not an effective search.

{{learner-b}} first sets an objective and picks keywords, then searches the discovery tool, glances over the results to judge which look suitable, and follows a reference from the best one to a further source. The search moved through the stages in order. This is an effective, planned search.

Both students searched the same tool. Only {{learner-b}} worked through the stages that make a search effective.

_items.text: Have I planned the search by setting a clear objective?
Have I chosen keywords that capture my topic?
Have I used my library's discovery service, rather than only a general search engine?
Have I weighed whether the sources I found are suitable, rather than taking the first?
Have I followed a lead to extend the search to further material?
Have I treated the search as a process, rather than a single lookup?

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The key term: keyword
definition: A word or short phrase you use when searching, chosen to capture the heart of your topic.
extendedDefinition: Keywords drive a search. The search tool looks for the words you give it, so the words you choose decide what you find. Changing a keyword, or adding a synonym, changes your results.
example: For a search on how sleep affects memory, the keywords might be 'sleep', 'memory' and 'learning'.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students plan a search on the same topic: whether using a phone before bed affects sleep.

{{learner-a}} types the sentence 'does using a phone before bed affect sleep' straight into the search box. The results are thin and off-topic. {{learner-a}} has not set an objective or chosen keywords: the whole question has gone in as one long phrase, so the tool struggles to match it. This is searching without a plan.

{{learner-b}} first sets the objective, recent research on screen use and sleep, then picks keywords: 'phone', 'sleep' and 'screen'. Noticing that 'phone' could also be 'smartphone' or 'mobile', {{learner-b}} adds those synonyms to catch more. The search returns relevant material. This is a planned search with well-chosen keywords.

Both students searched the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} planned the search and chose keywords, with synonyms to broaden it.

_incorrect.final: A synonym for 'children' is a word with much the same meaning, such as 'young people' or 'kids'. The other options name a chapter, a phrase, or a place, not the same idea.

body: What best describes academic searching, compared with the everyday searching you do online?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best describes academic searching compared with everyday searching?

_items.text: It is exploratory, iterative and strategy-driven, rather than a quick single lookup.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is what sets academic searching apart.

_items.text: It is exactly the same, just done on a library website.
_items.feedback: The place is not the difference; how you search is.

_items.text: It means always taking the first result you are given.
_items.feedback: That is the everyday approach, not the academic one.

_items.text: It means reading every source you can find on a topic.
_items.feedback: Reading everything is not the aim; a planned, exploratory search is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic searching is exploratory, iterative and strategy-driven.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how academic searching differs from a quick everyday lookup.

body: Which of these is a feature of academic searching but not usually of everyday searching?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a feature of academic searching but not everyday searching?

_items.text: Trying some keywords, seeing the results, and searching again with better ones.
_items.feedback: Yes. Searching again with better words is the iterative habit of academic searching.

_items.text: Typing a question and reading the first answer.
_items.feedback: That is everyday searching.

_items.text: Expecting a single fact as the answer.
_items.feedback: Everyday searching often seeks one fact; academic searching follows a question.

_items.text: Finishing in a few seconds.
_items.feedback: Speed is typical of everyday searching, not a feature of academic searching.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic searching is iterative: you search again with better words.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the habit that belongs to a planned, exploratory search.

body: Effective searching is best described as...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Effective searching is best described as...

_items.text: a planned process that moves through stages.
_items.feedback: Yes. Effective searching is a staged, planned process.

_items.text: a single lookup that ends at the first result.
_items.feedback: A one-off lookup skips the stages of an effective search.

_items.text: typing the same words repeatedly until something appears.
_items.feedback: Repeating the same words is not a process.

_items.text: gathering the largest possible number of sources.
_items.feedback: Quantity is not what makes a search effective.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Effective searching is a planned process with stages.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option describes a planned process?

body: A student runs one search, gets poor results, and gives up. Which principle of effective searching have they missed?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which principle of effective searching has the student missed?

_items.text: That searching is a process: you adjust your keywords and search again.
_items.feedback: Yes. Effective searching is iterative and planned, not a single attempt.

_items.text: That you must always use the longest source available.
_items.feedback: Source length is not a principle of effective searching.

_items.text: That the first result is always the best one.
_items.feedback: Taking the first result is the weak approach, not a principle.

_items.text: That searching should always be finished in one step.
_items.feedback: A single step is the one-off lookup an effective search avoids.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student missed that searching is an iterative, planned process.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The student stopped after one attempt; which principle does that break?

body: When planning a search, what should you decide before you start typing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you decide before typing when planning a search?

_items.text: Your objective, and what sort of source would answer it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Planning starts with an objective and the kind of source you need.

_items.text: How long your finished essay will be.
_items.feedback: Essay length is not part of planning a search.

_items.text: Which result you will choose before you have searched.
_items.feedback: You cannot choose a result before searching; planning sets your objective.

_items.text: How many tabs you will open at once.
_items.feedback: Opening tabs is not planning a search.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Planning starts with an objective and the sort of source you need.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option is about setting up the search before you type?

body: One of your keywords is 'car'. Which of these is a synonym you could add to broaden the search?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a synonym for 'car' to broaden the search?

_items.text: 'Automobile' or 'vehicle'.
_items.feedback: Yes. A synonym means much the same thing, so it catches different wording for the same idea.

_items.text: 'Page five'.
_items.feedback: That names a part of a document, not another word for the same idea.

_items.text: 'Next week'.
_items.feedback: That is unrelated to the keyword; it is not a synonym.

_items.text: 'Search engine'.
_items.feedback: That names a tool you search with, not a synonym for 'car'.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A synonym such as 'automobile' broadens the search to catch different wording.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A synonym means much the same as the keyword; which option does that?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what academic searching is, the principles of an effective search, and how to plan a search and choose keywords. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to search like an expert. The aim is to see these three ideas as one practice you work through each time you search, rather than three separate ideas. Build the habit now and it carries on past this course, into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how what academic searching is, the principles of an effective search, and planning with keywords connect as one searching practice
show the whole searching practice at work in a worked example of finding sources
plan one way to use the three together on your next search in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: Academic searching is one practice you work through, not three separate skills. You know it is exploratory, iterative and planned, rather than a quick lookup. You know an effective search moves through stages. And you make the first moves yourself: you set an objective and choose keywords, with a synonym or two. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are parts of that one practice, and you use them together each time you search.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this means bringing the three ideas to every search, in any subject. You decide what you are looking for, choose keywords with a synonym or two, then search and weigh what comes back. The search that uses the whole practice almost always beats the one typed in on a whim. Over a term, making this your normal way of searching is what steadily improves the sources you find.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a search you have coming up for your course. How will you use the whole practice on it, from deciding what you want to weighing the sources, and where will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Academic searching is most useful when you treat it as one practice, not three separate ideas. You bring the same moves to every search: know what you are looking for, plan, choose keywords, then search and weigh what you find. Making this your normal way of searching is what steadily improves the sources you rely on.

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: Searching is one practice you work through each time, not three separate skills. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Set an aim
_items.body: Decide what you are looking for and set a clear objective, so you know a good source when you see one.

_items.title: Choose keywords
_items.body: Choose keywords that capture your objective, and think of a synonym or two in case the first words come up short.

_items.title: Search
_items.body: Search, look at what comes back, and try again with better words. A first search rarely lands it.

_items.title: Weigh sources
_items.body: Weigh the sources you find, and keep the ones you can trust for the work in hand.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students each need sources for the same assignment. Student A types the whole question into a search box and uses the first result, with no plan and no second look. Student B uses the whole practice instead: deciding what they want, choosing keywords with a synonym, searching, then weighing the sources. Both spent time searching, but Student B found clearer, more trustworthy material, because the search used every part of the practice.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to search as one practice
body: Use these to check you have searched as one practice, not just part of it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I decide what I was looking for before I started typing?
Did I choose keywords, with a synonym or two, rather than the whole question?
Did I treat the first results as a start, and search again with better words?
Did I weigh the sources I found, rather than taking the first one?
Will I use this same planned practice on my next search?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat searching as one practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat searching as one practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat searching as one practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because the three ideas connect: knowing what searching is shapes how you plan, and planning shapes the keywords you choose and search with.
_items.feedback: Yes. The ideas connect, so using them together makes each one work better.

_items.text: Because getting one idea right means you can skip the other two.
_items.feedback: No. The point is that the ideas connect, not that any one replaces the rest.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to plan a search or choose keywords.
_items.feedback: Not so. Planning and keywords are part of the one practice, not things it removes.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less thought than three separate ideas.
_items.feedback: The gain is not less thought. It is that the ideas feed one another.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Searching is one practice whose parts feed one another, used together each time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how each idea sets up the next one.

displayTitle: A student decides what they are looking for, chooses keywords with a synonym, searches, and weighs the sources before using them. What does this show?
body: A student decides what they are looking for, chooses keywords with a synonym, searches, and weighs the sources before using them. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student decides what they are looking for, chooses keywords with a synonym, searches, and weighs the sources before using them. What does this show?

_items.text: That they are using the whole searching practice: the three ideas working together, from deciding what they want to weighing what they find.
_items.feedback: Yes. Every idea is there, working together as one practice.

_items.text: That they are doing more than any search really needs.
_items.feedback: No. Each part does a different job, and together they make the search stronger.

_items.text: That only the keywords really matter in a search.
_items.feedback: Not so. Keywords are one part of the practice, not the whole of it.

_items.text: That weighing the sources is the same as planning the search.
_items.feedback: They are different parts: planning comes first, and weighing the sources comes later.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student used the whole practice, the three ideas working together.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Notice how the student uses every idea, not just one.

displayTitle: You want to use this whole practice to find better sources for {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats searching as one practice?
body: You want to use this whole practice to find better sources for {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats searching as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this whole practice to find better sources for your subject this term. Which plan best treats searching as one practice?

_items.text: On each search, decide what you want and set an objective, choose keywords with a synonym, then search and weigh what you find.
_items.feedback: Yes. That uses every part of the practice, together, each time you search.

_items.text: Type your whole assignment title into the first search box and use the top result.
_items.feedback: That drops planning, keywords and weighing the sources, which is where the work happens.

_items.text: Only plan the searches you find hard, and skip planning on the rest.
_items.feedback: Planning is part of the one practice you use every time, not only when a search feels hard.

_items.text: Choose plenty of keywords and keep every source the search returns.
_items.feedback: Keywords are only one part, and keeping every source skips weighing what you find.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The whole practice, used together, is what you bring to every search.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that uses every part, not just one.

_items.text: Decide what they are looking for, choose keywords with a synonym, then search and weigh the sources before using them.
